newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS--Gasoline leads oils up, coffee and platinum rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS--Gasoline leads oils up, coffee and platinum rise.

text.p: Gasoline prices rose sharply for a second straight day on Monday as traders worried about supply disruptions at home and abroad pushed up prices.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline for September delivery closed 1.67 cents a gallon higher at 66.74 cents. The strength carried over to other oil markets, with September crude oil ending up 47 cents at $20.75 a barrel and September heating oil up 1.88 cents at 58.44 cents a gallon.
"Gasoline is continuing higher because of the same story: high demand amid refinery outages," said Tom Bentz, analyst and trader with High Yield Analytics Inc in New York.
Gasoline supplies have been tightened by both domestic and foreign production disruptions, boosting prices 6 cents a gallon in the last week.

Last Wednesday, refiner Tosco Corp shut down the catalytic cracking unit at its 250,000 barrel per day Bayway refinery in New Jersey due to a leakage. The facility may be shut down through mid-August or longer, traders said.
Overseas, the 60,000 barrel a day Coryton catalytic cracker in the U.K. operated by British Petroleum and Mobil Corp was still shut down on Monday for maintenance following technical problems.

Crude oil supplies from Colombia have also been disrupted. Occidental Petroleum, operator of the Cano Limon field which produces an average 175,000 barrels a day, shut down the field on Monday after a weekend landslide partially destroyed the pipeline that pumps crude from field to tanker terminal.

The disruptions allowed oil traders to shrug of fresh indications that Iraq would soon be able to begin selling crude oil for another six months under a United Nations deal that allows it to raise fund to buy food and other supplies.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Monday approved an Iraqi distribution plan, clearing the way for oil sales.

"Crude and heating oil were being sold short in anticipation of the U.N. approval of the plan. After the news, crude and heat did not sell off that much, so traders covered their short positions to catch up with gasoline," said Bentz.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee prices also rose sharply on concerns about a shortage of quality supplies.
Coffee for September delivery closed up 8.80 cents a pound at 193.75 cents.
"The one thing that is driving this market is anxiety about there being enough coffee for September delivery," said Refco Inc analyst Ann Prendergast.

Some traders speculated that roaster demand will pick up in the coming weeks ahead of the peak winter consumption season in North America. But concerns surfaced about a shortage of premium coffees available until the start of the new harvest in many Latin American countries this autumn.
"There's not going to be much coffee around for when demand picks up," said South Futures president Stephen Smith. "And right now there is no reason to sell it. There's no coffee to be hedged."
Platinum and palladium prices also continued to surge on supply worries.

September palladium at the NYMEX ended up $9.00 at $215.60 an ounce, a new life-of-contract high for a second straight day. Spot palladium was quoted at $239.00 an ounce in London, only $1.00 an ounce below the 17-year high set on June 6.
October platinum ended up $16.70 at $455.20 an ounce, with spot platinum in London quoted at $448.00 an ounce, compared to the seven-year high of near $500.00 seen in early June.
Russia suspended platinum group metals (PGM) exports in December before resuming some shipments last month. Russia supplies about 60 percent of the world's palladium and 20 percent of its platinum.

"Doubts about Russia as a reliable supplier, uncertainty over the size of the Russian PGM stockpile, and reports of a power struggle for control of Russian PGM exports between the Russian precious metals export agency, the Finance Ministry, producer Norilsk Nikel, and the central bank, should keep the supply outlook problematic," said Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.
